headlines.title: Surveillance video shows moment ICE agent's gun found in San Francisco airport bathroom
headlines.description: Surveillance video from San Francisco International Airport obtained by NBC Bay Area is shedding more light on a July incident where an ICE deportation officer allegedly left his gun unattended in an airport restroom. A review of roughly two hours of CCTV footage – obtained through a California Public Records Act request – shows the moment the gun was found inside a bathroom stall by a flight attendant, along with the likely moment the ICE agent returned to the scene roughly 10 minutes later. As NBC Bay Area first reported in August, the firearm was found unattended inside a bathroom stall past security checkpoint D in Terminal 2, according to airport spokesperson Doug Yakel. Around 10:23 p.m., the surveillance video shows a person who appears to be the flight attendant run out of the bathroom and flag down airport security. The flight attendant and security officer then head back to the bathroom. Airport security then calls 9-1-1 and reports the gun to San Francisco police. “Hi, yeah, a flight attendant just came up to me and said there is a gun in the men’s bathroom,” an airport security officer tells police in a recording of the 9-1-1 call. San Francisco Aug 26 San Francisco Aug 27 The video shows additional law enforcement officers quickly arrive to investigate. Multiple travelers are turned away from the bathroom by police or security. The video makes it clear that dozens of people could potentially have found the gun if the flight attendant had not spotted it and notified security. Roughly 10 minutes after the flight attendant appears to discover the gun, the surveillance video shows a man dressed in plain clothes approach security outside the bathroom, present what looks like a badge, and enter the bathroom. A few minutes later, police report that an ICE agent has come back to the bathroom to retrieve the gun, according to a recording of police radio traffic. “I have a gentleman here who just arrived, claiming this is his firearm,” someone says in the recording. “He’s a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation officer.” The video shows the apparent ICE agent emerge from the bathroom more than 10 minutes later with other law enforcement officials. He remains in front of the bathroom, where he seems to talk to officers on scene and present some sort of identification. Police radio traffic shows officers verify the person who came back to retrieve the firearm is an ICE officer and that the gun belongs to him. “We verified his firearm serial number through the government website,” someone says in a recording of the dispatch audio. Due to the position of the video camera and the quality of the video, it was not immediately clear to NBC Bay Area when the agent may have first left the gun in the bathroom. For weeks, NBC Bay Area has been asking ICE if the agent has faced any discipline for misplacing his gun, but the agency has not responded. NBC Bay Area also asked both ICE and SFO on Friday to confirm if the man in the video is, in fact, the ICE agent, but has not received a response.
headlines.source: Hilda Gutierrez, Michael Bott and Alex Bozovic

headlines.title: Mountain lion released back into the wild after being captured in San Francisco
headlines.description: A young mountain lion was released back into the wild Friday after it was safely captured in San Francisco’s Sunset District. The mountain lion in the morning was spotted in yards and on a street. Video also showed the mountain lion on 44th Avenue. Neighbors said the animal moved from one bush to another in front of homes and stayed there. Police, animal control and other agencies responded. The street was blocked off and neighbors were told to stay back as officials worked to tranquilize the mountain lion. The California Department of Fish and Wildlife said the mountain lion was darted and ran off before the tranquilizer took effect. Officials then performed a quick health assessment and determined the animal was a male between 2 and 3 years old and weighed roughly 78 pounds. It was a morning that neighbors won’t soon forget. “It ran right in front of our house, and then they tranquilized it, and we saw it run out into the street too,” San Francisco resident Alex Grant said. “It was wild to see a mountain lion in a big city like this. It’s pretty incredible,” Grant added. Another neighbor, Carson Ryan, said he came to the area after seeing the police response. “I made my way over here at 10 o’clock. That’s when I saw all the police cars, caution tape, and I hung around and wanted to see what was really a mountain lion in the Outer Sunset, which it was,” Ryan said. After the mountain lion was safely captured, Fish and Wildlife officials placed a tracking collar on it and returned it to the wild. Officials said they are not sure where the mountain lion came from, but it could have traveled from the Peninsula, where there is habitat. headlines.title: Humpback whale spotted swimming in Sacramento River
headlines.description: A humpback whale has been spotted swimming in the California Delta, with new video capturing the animal near the Rio Vista Bridge. The whale was originally spotted Tuesday near the Richmond shipping channel. On Wednesday afternoon, a man fishing near the Rio Vista Bridge in Rio Vista captured video of the whale. He said he initially thought his friend was mistaken about seeing it. The Delta is no stranger to whales. In 1985, a whale named Humphrey spent several weeks in the Rio Vista area before eventually returning to the ocean. In 2007, a mother whale and her calf also spent several weeks in the Delta. Scientists are asking people to keep their distance from the whale.

headlines.title: San Jose mayor meets with neighbors complaining about data center noise
headlines.description: On Wednesday night, Mayor Matt Mahan met with some South San Jose residents who say they’ve been dealing with a low, constant hum and bright lights shinning into their backyards coming from data centers nearby. Neighbors said the noise can get even louder when temperatures rise. Their concerns come as San Jose looks at whether its rules for data centers need to be strengthened. Denisa and Jay Filichia live in South San Jose. Their backyard faces several data centers along Great Oaks Boulevard, separated by a few roads and train tracks. “We’re not anti-data center at all, it’s more the noise and the lights that are bothering us,” Filichia said. Denisa has been in contact with the city, and on Wednesday night, Mayor Matt Mahan went to the neighborhood to hear the noise for himself. The mayor and the neighbors then walked toward Monterey Road, getting closer to the data centers. The neighbors’ complaints come as data centers themselves are facing increased scrutiny in other cities as these facilities usually require significant amounts of electricity and water, causing a lot of anger in some communities. Some are even imposing temporary moratoriums on new data centers, all together. San Jose hasn’t. The city is hearing from residents and considering stronger standards. “We should require that if a data center in San Jose can access our purple pipe, that’s our recycled water network, that they need to hook up to that system and become a customer and pay for that water,” Mahan said. Mahan says that would also help the city expand its recycled water system. And for Denisa and Jay, he says he’ll work with the data centers to try to address the noise and light. “We’ll talk to them. Maybe they can put some insulation or shielding around the fans and quiet down on their end. maybe we can turn down the lights,” Mahan said. San Jose plans to hold a series of town halls in the coming months as it works on potential new standards and regulations for those data centers. As for any proposed rules they come up with, they’re expected to come before the San Jose City Council in December.

headlines.title: Partial Hwy. 101 closures expected to cause weekend delays in SF, San Rafael
headlines.description: Caltrans will close all northbound lanes of U.S. Highway 101 between Cesar Chavez and 17th streets in San Francisco beginning Friday night for work on the Hospital Curve rehabilitation project. Starting at 11 p.m, the closure will be in effect through the weekend and is scheduled to reopen by 6 a.m. Monday. More closures are planned for Oct. 2-4 and Oct. 16-18. Also at 11 p.m., Caltrans will close northbound Highway 101 lanes at the Harbor Bridge in San Rafael for a structural improvement project. The lanes are expected to reopen by 6 a.m. Saturday, with overnight closures continuing through Monday. Detour information during Highway 101 closure in San Francisco Interstate 280 will be the main alternative during the northbound Hwy. 101 closure. Caltrans said I‑280 northbound is suggested for travel toward downtown San Francisco or the Bay Bridge. Public transportation is also highly encouraged to bypass congestion and avoid work‑zone delays. headlines.title: Moss Landing Power Plant fire started in batteries not removed after 2025 fire
headlines.description: A fire that sparked Friday at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County ignited in batteries that had not yet been removed after a larger fire at the same facility in January 2025. The county issued shelter-in-place orders within a third of a mile of the Vistra battery energy storage facility at the power plant at 7301 state Highway 1 after the fire was first reported around 6:15 a.m. Friday. Those orders have since been lifted. Authorities held a midday briefing to provide an update on the fire, which is expected to burn itself out by Saturday and involved batteries that had not yet been removed from the site after the larger fire on Jan. 16, 2025. Jess Cortez, fire chief with the North County Fire Protection District said the batteries were inaccessible after the 2025 fire because they were along a wall at risk of collapse. After they caught fire Friday, Cortez said the “best tactic is to let these batteries burn themselves out.” The batteries were still energized but were idle and that unit had been disconnected from the electric grid after the 2025 fire, according to Ron George, manager of the Vistra plant in Moss Landing. George acknowledged that until all batteries are removed from the site, there is a possibility of future flareups like the one that occurred Friday. Monterey County Jul 25 Monterey County Apr 28, 2025 Investigative Unit Mar 25, 2025 The shelter-in-place orders in the immediate vicinity of the facility remained in place until Friday afternoon. Authorities had also initially instructed students and staff at some schools in the area to stay inside Friday morning, but eventually allowed students to go outside. No injuries have been reported in connection with the fire. Monterey County Supervisor Glenn Church, who represents the Moss Landing area, has led multiple community meetings about the 2025 fire and resulting investigation and said he is “deeply disappointed and frustrated” at having to deal with another fire at the same site. Church said the fire underscores how volatile the battery storage systems can be and said it is “troublesome for the community when this continues to come up.” Officials with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Monterey Bay Air Resources District have been monitoring sensors around the facility and said they did not show readings out of the ordinary Friday. A meteorologist with the National Weather Service said light winds and a marine layer kept smoke from the fire from spreading very far. The cause of the 2025 fire has not been released and authorities did not say what might have sparked Friday’s new blaze. The EPA earlier in September said it was starting the final phase of battery cleanup and demolition of the battery storage building and was going to “take every precaution to mitigate the risk of a fire incident on-site.” Prior to Friday’s fire, the EPA had estimated that the battery removal and building demolition process would be complete by mid-2027. Monterey County sheriff’s spokesperson Cmdr. Andres Rosas said there was no estimate yet for when the shelter-in-place orders will be lifted. “We will update the community as soon as we make a decision,” Rosas said. Speaker of the Assembly Robert Rivas issued the following statement on the fire: “The safety of our Central Coast community is always a top priority, and my team is closely monitoring the battery storage facility fire at Moss Landing. We are grateful to the firefighters and first responders on the scene, and our office is receiving regular updates. If you live in the area, please follow all emergency guidance and warnings, and heed the directions of local officials. Thanks again to the brave first responders and emergency personnel always working to protect our community.”

headlines.title: SF Opera, orchestra settle strike as performances resume Tuesday
headlines.description: The San Francisco Opera and the San Francisco Opera Orchestra have reached a tentative contract agreement and performances in the 2026-27 season will begin next week. The agreement between management and members of the American Federation of Musicians Union Local 6 was reached Thursday, following a strike that began one week ago which caused the cancellation of season-opening performances. The new contract, covering Aug. 1 of this year through July 31, 2030, is still subject to ratification. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, whose office assisted with negotiations, said, “I am grateful to the musicians of Local 6 for their constant commitment to reaching an agreement, and I want to thank Matthew Shilvock and the San Francisco Opera leadership for their hard work throughout the process. We would not have an agreement without the dedication of Matthew Goudeau, our executive director of arts and culture, who spent night after night in City Hall and the War Memorial, working to get the opera started again.” The 104th season opens Tuesday with Giuseppe Verdi’s “Simon Boccanegra” in Claus Guth’s Hamburg State Opera production, staged for San Francisco Opera by revival director Katherine M. Carter. Thea Musgrave’s “Mary, Queen of Scots,” which had its West Coast premiere in 1979 under the composer’s baton, opens Thursday in a new co-production with English National Opera directed by Stewart Laing and led by debuting conductor Clelia Cafiero. Ticketholders for canceled dates of “Simon Boccanegra” and “Mary, Queen of Scots” have various options: They may apply the ticket value to purchase tickets for an upcoming performance in the 2026-27 season; they may donate the value or may request a refund by visiting https://www.sfopera.com/updates or calling the box office at 415-864-3330.

headlines.title: Councilwoman receives death threats and assaulted over Pittsburg data center
headlines.description: A Pittsburg councilwoman says she’s gotten death threats and was recently assaulted over the city’s approved data center. “When they become threatening to us. When they become violent. I say that because I was assaulted,” Councilmember Arlene Kobata said on a podcast. Kobata said the woman, angry over the city approving a data center, assaulted her at a public event. “She grabbed me and shoved me a couple of times, and had some strong words with me,” she said. Kobata says that’s not the only scary incident she’s experienced as the community has become increasingly fired up over the 77-acre data center set to be built on the former site of a golf course. She says she and others have received harassing emails and even death threats. Kobata was a member of the planning commission who agreed the project is compliant with California environmental regulations. She insists the center will not be a drain on natural resources. The threats are drawing criticism from many in the community, includingPittsburg’smayor, who points out the city has paused further action while it conducts community outreach. In a statement, Mayor Dionne Adams said, “Violence against anyone is never the answer. We can disagree passionately, but we must do so peacefully and ensure every resident has a safe and meaningful opportunity to be heard.” Kobata insists the data center will not harm the community and says she was not on council when it was approved. She also says she won’t let the threats silence her. “We’re tough we’re still gonna stand tough for what we believe is right for the residents,” she said.

headlines.title: Security guards at Bay Area tech companies join statewide strike
headlines.description: Nearly 14,000 security guards across California walked off the job Friday morning as they demand higher pay, better health care benefits and safer working conditions. The strike began around 4:30 a.m., just as Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference came to a close in San Francisco. About 50,000 people from major tech companies attended Dreamforce over the past three days. Companies including Salesforce, Google, OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are among those that use contracted security guards and could be impacted by the walkout. The guards work for major security companies including Allied Universal, GardaWorld and Securitas and are represented by the Service Employees International Union. Those security companies provide guards to tech firms and events such as Dreamforce. Union members voted Tuesday to authorize the strike and later announced on social media that the walkout would begin Friday morning. The union accuses the security companies of engaging in bad-faith bargaining, illegally surveilling guards and unfairly retaliating against employees. The guards are seeking a path toward wages of $30 an hour. According to a UC Berkeley study cited by the union, guards currently earn about $20 an hour. They are also seeking better health care benefits, which the union says have not kept pace with the cost of living or the demands of the job. Other demands include safer working conditions and an end to what the union describes as unfair labor practices. The union is negotiating with the security companies, not the tech firms that contract with them. No specific picketing locations had been announced as of Friday morning.

headlines.title: Brentwood community mourns Liberty High School students killed in crash
headlines.description: The Liberty High School community in Brentwood gathered on Thursday to remember two students killed in a crash over the weekend. Caden Kyle and Dominic Ferrari were killed in a crash near Deer Valley and Balfour roads just after midnight Sunday A third Liberty High School student remains hospitalized in critical condition. The school’s principal Efa Huckaby says even those who didn’t know the students personally were feeling the pain. “A lot of the community, even if they didn’t know the young people, they’re still affected because it’s one of our own here,” he said. For some, the connection to Kyle and Ferrari goes back years, including friends who have known them since elementary school. The principal says bringing the school community together was important, to give students and families a place to grieve and lean on each other. “We like to think of Liberty High School as the center of the community, and so to be able to open our facilities for the families and for the students to have a space to grieve,” Huckaby said. Antioch police are leading the investigation into the crash. Investigators are asking anyone who may have witnessed what happened or has surveillance or dashcam video to come forward.

headlines.title: ‘We want answers': Family of Nvidia researcher continues to question suicide ruling
headlines.description: The family of a 32-year-old Nvidia researcher who died in July is calling on Palo Alto police to continue to dig into the circumstances of his death, which authorities have ruled a suicide. Irfan Al-Hussaini was found unresponsive in his Palo Alto home on July 22 and died about a week later. His family is urging state and local authorities to look further into his death, saying the circumstances surrounding his passing are suspicious. “The brother I knew would never, ever take his own life,” Irfan’s sister, Sarah Al-Hussaini, said Thursday during a news conference in front of Palo Alto City Hall. Irfan was a senior AI researcher at Nvidia who had recently been promoted and was focused on his promising future. While authorities ruled his death a suicide, his family argues the evidence they have says otherwise. “What little information we were told does not match with the information we have gathered so far and the things we know,” Sarah said. The family said Irfan presented research to about 15 colleagues until about 9 a.m. on July 22. At 10:02 a.m., a Slack message was sent from his account to his manager saying his wife was not feeling well and would take the day off, the family said. A 911 call was placed about 20 minutes later. Doctors told the family initial scans suggested Irfan had been without oxygen for nearly 30 to 60 minutes. “So who sent that 10:02 text?” Sarah said. “Does that text fit with the medical timeline?” The family and their attorney, Tony Brass, said there was no suicide note left. They also question whether domestic violence was overlooked. “The plan that they’re supposed to accept is that he hung himself from a door while his wife was home and he did it in a way that she did not detect or know that that was happening,” Brass said. “That makes no sense.” The family said Irfan was wearing an Oura ring that morning and believes its data could potentially help establish a timeline for investigators. “We want a proper investigation, we want answers, we want justice for Irfan,” Sarah said. Palo Alto police said the case remains under investigation, pending the medical examiner’s report. The department said it has received materials from the family and others, adding that neither police nor the medical examiner have identified evidence of foul play. An attorney for Irfan’s widow said she fully cooperated with the investigation and that a full forensic autopsy was performed on Aug. 31. The attorney said Irfan’s widow has no objections to forensic materials being reviewed. If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline or chat live at 988lifeline.org. You can also visit SpeakingOfSuicide.com/resources for additional support.

headlines.title: Berkeley's Triple Rock Brewery to close after 40 years in downtown
headlines.description: A beloved brewery in downtown Berkeley has announced that it is planning to close after four decades of operations. Triple Rock Brewery and Taphouse on Shattuck Avenue will close by the end of the year, its owners wrote in a post on the brewery’s website. The business opened in 1986, originally called Roaring Rock Brewery. The owners, brothers John and Martin Reid, say this is the oldest, continuously operating brewpub in the U.S. In the post on the website, the owners said they are ready to retire. The owners told SF Gate that the general decline in alcohol sales also contributed to their decision to close. The brewpub will remain open until the end of the Cal Berkeley semester in December, patrons are encouraged to come by and share memories before this chapter closes.
